title: Who's the greatest? (Mark 9:30–37)
hookLine: they argue about rank; he puts a child in the middle
carry: last of all, servant of all

lines: A SECOND WARNING ON THE ROAD.
cards: What were you arguing about back there? Ask that after a long car ride with kids in the back seat, and you get silence. Everyone suddenly fascinated by the window.

That's this scene. Jesus is passing quietly through Galilee, and for the second time he tells his friends he'll be handed over and killed, and rise the third day. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask.
Then, in the house in Capernaum, he asks what they were arguing about on the road.
Mark tells us, in the King James Bible: "But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed among themselves, who should be the greatest."

teach.h: ARGUING ABOUT RANK ON THE WAY.
teach.b: Notice the timing. He has just told them he's going to suffer and die, and they spend the walk arguing about who's number one. Mark doesn't soften it.

teach.h: LAST OF ALL, SERVANT OF ALL.
teach.b: He sits down, calls the twelve over, and says: "If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all."

teach.h: DIAKONOS: THE ONE WHO WAITS TABLES.
teach.b: The Greek word for servant is diakonos, the one who waits on tables. It's where the church later got the word deacon. The ladder turns upside down: the greatest is the one bringing the plates.
He takes a child, stands the child in the middle of the circle of grown men, and takes the child up in his arms.

Whoever welcomes one little child like this in my name, he says, welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. A small child can do nothing for anyone's rank. Welcoming one wins you nothing.
That seems to be the point.

teach.h: THE SAME SHALL BE LAST OF ALL, AND SERVANT OF ALL.
teach.b: Churches still meet this in ordinary ways: who gets the seat at the front, who serves the coffee, who is noticed. The argument on the road is very old, and very ordinary.
And his answer is sitting in the middle of the room, in his arms.

how: Churches of many traditions have deacons, a word from the Greek for servant, who care for the poor and help at worship, and some Christians point to this passage when talking about leadership as service.

o: a church elder who rules a congregation
a messenger sent out to carry the news
a servant, the one who waits on tables

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: last of all, servant of all

s: the disciples admitted what they'd argued about
they held their peace. Mark tells us what it was.
the word deacon comes from the Greek for servant
diakonos, one who waits on tables.
the argument came right after he spoke of his death
the second warning, on the same road.

games.q: you're Jesus. you've just told your friends you will suffer, and they spent the walk arguing about rank. what do you do?
o: rebuke them sharply and walk off.
sit down and put a child in the middle.
name the greatest to end the argument.
games.why: he sits, teaches that the first must be last and servant of all, and takes a child in his arms.

practice: Think of someone younger than you whom you'll see today: a child, a grandchild, a student, a new person at work, the youngest in the family chat.
What would serving them look like: listening to the whole long story, making them something, asking their opinion and meaning it? Choose one thing, and if you pray, hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: Diakonos, the Greek word for servant, the one who waits on tables. The argument on the road. His answer: the last of all, the servant of all, and a child in the middle.

orig.note: Greek: a servant, especially one who waits at table. the root of the English deacon.

carryVoice: Your line: last of all, servant of all. The way up is the way down. That's day one hundred ninety-seven.
